title: Some Tests Are Really Great for Students
author: Stuart Jr., Dave
summary: Dave Stuart Jr. pushes back on the reflexive vilification of testing by describing a test he considers good: the AP World History exam taken by his ninth graders. He argues it is fair because it derives from a published course description, all teachers can aim at it, and everyone sits the same exam under the same conditions. It is also demanding, requiring students to make thousands of facts retrievable across geography, chronology and themes and to build conceptual understanding from them. Meaningful stakes, which for his students ranged from college credit to family pride to simply testing their limits, supplied the motivation. He insists the students were not beholden to scorecards but content at having done their best at a hard thing. The piece makes a measured case that fairness, challenge and real stakes together make an assessment valuable rather than harmful.
points: Tests earn their bad reputation from poor design and bogus stakes, not from assessment as such.
Fairness here comes from transparency: a published course description, released tests and a single standardized sitting.
The challenge works because students must organize retrievable knowledge in several ways and then synthesize it into conceptual understanding.
Stakes motivate when they are personal, such as seeing what one is capable of, rather than only about credit or teacher evaluation.
quotes: Tests are easy to vilify in the USA today because there are too many bad ones and there are too many bogus high stakes attached to them. But this school year I’ve seen an extremely difficult test have a profoundly positive effect on its takers.

Yet the AP test had a profound effect on this precious mishmash of kids. For the first time in my career, my students had a beautifully fair, exceptionally challenging assessment with meaningful stakes at the end of my course.

The APWH test is fair because it’s drawn from a 133-page course description, and fifty percent of its score is based on essay questions that can be answered using a wide variety of world history knowledge. Every APWH teacher has access to the course description, and every APWH teacher’s goal is to craft their course according to it.

You learn thousands of pieces of information during the school year, and you have to figure out how to make many of them retrievable. That retrievability needs to be organized geographically, chronologically, and thematically, too.

And finally, all this data, understood from various angles, together needs to produce deeper conceptual understandings of world history. It’s not an impossible test, but it’s one that requires more out of my students than many of them believed they could give at the start of the school year.

Sure, to some of my kids the college credit was why they cared. But to others, the stakes were simply that they wanted to see what they were capable of. Others wanted to make their family members proud; some desired to “make history” by being the ever-so-rare student who scores a 5 as a ninth grader.
